content: A survey involving 178 healthcare workers, with 37% from the WHO Africa Region, revealed that 79% supported expanding access to antiviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of hepatitis B virus (HBV). However, only 59% of these healthcare workers currently offered antiviral prophylaxis to pregnant women in their respective settings. The barriers identified included a lack of policies (78%), limited access to HBV DNA testing (73%), insufficient staff training (73%), and refusal by pregnant women (16%). A 2023 WHO survey of 41 national hepatitis program managers from 33 countries showed that 71% strongly supported expanding eligibility for antiviral prophylaxis to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women in settings without access to HBV DNA testing. Program managers highlighted the limited availability and high out-of-pocket costs of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and the lack of HBV testing in early pregnancy as major obstacles to expanding antiviral prophylaxis for PMTCT in their countries. The implementation of the 2020 WHO recommendation to offer TDF prophylaxis to HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA levels or positive HBeAg, in addition to the hepatitis B birth dose, has been hindered by poor access to HBV DNA and HBeAg assays. Expanding TDF prophylaxis to all HBsAg-positive pregnant women in settings without HBV DNA access could significantly improve equity in access, but this would require affordable and readily available TDF. In settings with access to HBV DNA or HBeAg assays, the 2020 recommendation to use TDF prophylaxis only for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL remains applicable. In countries without such access, particularly those with low uptake of the hepatitis B birth dose vaccine, universal prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive women offers a feasible pathway to address ongoing HBV mother-to-child transmission (MTCT). However, this approach necessitates clear communication of the benefits and risks to childbearing women. Following the introduction of universal hepatitis B infant vaccination in China in 1992, the SHIELD project was initiated to scale up immunoprophylaxis for hepatitis B among infants in 10 hospitals. This was followed by a nationwide hospital-based implementation study for HBV PMTCT, including antiviral prophylaxis for highly viremic pregnant women, and later expanded to community-level interventions such as electronic clinics offering one-stop services. Generic TDF is available at low cost, but access to monotherapy remains challenging in some countries. TDF is also available as part of fixed-dose combinations (e.g., TDF + 3TC or TDF + FTC) used in antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens or for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The market price for HBV DNA testing ranges from $15–50 in the Americas to $30–100 in the Western Pacific and African regions. Scaling up the hepatitis B birth dose is the most cost-effective option, delivering the greatest health benefits at the lowest cost. In countries with high birth dose coverage, adding antenatal testing and TDF prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive women may be cost-effective depending on diagnostic costs and implementation strategies. Several countries with high hepatitis B endemicity have achieved significant progress in controlling the disease through high infant vaccination coverage, including timely birth doses. However, HBV MTCT remains the primary mode of ongoing transmission globally. Peripartum antiviral prophylaxis programs have been initiated in most regions, but experience in the WHO African Region remains limited. Expanding antiviral therapy for HBV PMTCT will require increased timely birth dose coverage, universal testing for HBsAg, HIV, and syphilis in pregnant women, adequate sensitization and monitoring of pregnant women, increased healthcare worker capacity, robust procurement and supply chains for TDF, and good monitoring and evaluation systems. Universal antiviral prophylaxis for all HBsAg-positive women may be considered a temporary intervention to address ongoing MTCT while access to HBV DNA assays improves. Where HBV DNA testing is available, antiviral prophylaxis should be targeted to those with high HBV DNA levels at risk of transmission. Baseline HBV DNA testing for HBsAg-positive pregnant women enables a more complete assessment of treatment eligibility for their own health and informs decisions about lifelong treatment. Increasing access to lower-cost HBV DNA point-of-care assays or reliable HBeAg assays in antenatal clinics would make universal prophylaxis unnecessary. Integrated, simplified, and decentralized service delivery, including HIV, HBV, and syphilis testing and treatment pathways as part of antenatal services, will be key to implementing universal hepatitis B prophylaxis alongside scaling up birth dose and HepB3 coverage. WHO has launched criteria for validating the elimination of MTCT of HIV and syphilis, and triple elimination has been adopted in most WHO regions with developed healthcare systems. However, implementation with integrated antenatal care pathways is still in its early stages, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Accurate diagnostic strategies are needed to identify pregnant women with advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Although cirrhosis and HCC are uncommon during pregnancy, hepatitis B is a major cause, and both can have severe consequences for women and their babies. Since 2017, the use of FibroScan® during pregnancy is no longer contraindicated, but validated cut-offs for non-invasive tests for liver fibrosis in pregnant women are lacking. Biochemical markers such as APRI may not be accurate due to pregnancy-related hemodilution. Research gaps include evaluating the feasibility, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness of maternal peripartum antiviral prophylaxis (universal or high HBV DNA-driven) in settings without timely birth dose access, adherence to maternal prophylaxis, optimal timing and duration of TDF treatment, and follow-up studies on the benefits and risks of discontinuing versus continuing antiviral therapy postpartum. Evaluating different models of integrated antenatal hepatitis B care and triple elimination of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B is also needed. For adolescents aged 12–17 years with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), treatment is recommended for those with advanced liver disease, high HBV DNA levels with elevated ALT, or specific risk factors such as coinfections, family history of liver cancer, or comorbidities. Preferred antiviral regimens include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV), with alternatives such as TDF + lamivudine (3TC) or TDF + emtricitabine (FTC). For individuals with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function, entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) is recommended. Treatment for children aged 2–11 years is generally case-by-case, focusing on those with advanced liver disease or other risk factors.
